say.text: A 58-year-old woman has a thickened area in one breast that does not feel like a clear lump. Her biopsy shows small, uniform cells lined up one behind another, in single file. No mass is seen on mammography.
Which histological type is this?

choices.label: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Set aside how common each type is. Ask how the cells sit: do they form glands and a firm mass, or do they line up one behind another?
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because this is the commonest breast cancer, so it feels like the default answer to any type question.
But this type usually forms a hard, gritty mass, and the pattern here is cells in single file with no clear mass. Commonest is not the same as fits this picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the pattern before the frequency: the common type makes a mass, and this biopsy shows a line of cells.

say.text: Yes. Cells in single file, from loss of cell-to-cell adhesion, mark invasive lobular carcinoma.
You picked the pattern, not the frequency. Here is what the commonest type misses: it forms a firm, stellate mass, and lobular carcinoma often does not.
Lobular carcinoma is more often bilateral and multicentric, and it spreads unusually to the peritoneum, GI tract, ovaries and meninges.
ER or PR positive, HER2 negative, with low Ki-67, is Luminal A, the most common subtype.
A family with breast and ovarian cancers is being counselled. Before going further, you need the chromosome for each BRCA gene.
Which pair is correct?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match each gene to its own number first, then check the pair as a whole. A pair of numbers you remember can still have its owners swapped.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because you memorised 13 and 17 as one pair, so the two owners get swapped without you noticing.
Each gene has its own chromosome. The check is which gene owns which number, and the pair alone does not settle it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the trap: the numbers are the same, but the owners are not.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because 11 looks like one more number from the same memorised list, so it feels plausible.
Check each gene's chromosome against the claim, not against a number that merely looks familiar.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so test the number itself: a familiar-looking locus is not a remembered locus.

say.text: Yes. BRCA1 lies on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q.
You matched each gene to its own chromosome. Now the phenotype: BRCA1 is typically linked to triple-negative, basal-like tumours.
BRCA2 is the one more linked with male breast cancer, along with Klinefelter syndrome. Male breast cancer is about 1% of all breast cancers.
A man presents with a breast lump, and his family history includes breast cancer.
Which gene is most linked to breast cancer in men?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which gene is tied to the male form, not which gene is best known to the public.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because BRCA1 is the best-known breast cancer gene, so it feels like the answer to any hereditary question.
BRCA1 is tied to triple-negative tumours in women. Match the phenotype in the stem to the gene, not the gene you know best.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the famous-gene reflex: the stem names a phenotype, and the phenotype picks the gene.

say.text: Yes. BRCA2 carries the male breast cancer link, and Klinefelter syndrome is a second risk factor.
A 3 cm tumour lies under skin that looks like orange peel. The breast is not red or warm, and the whole breast is not swollen.
What causes the skin change?

choices.label: Tumour emboli in dermal lymphatics, as in inflammatory cancer
Blocked lymphatics under the skin, with oedema
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the lymph channels just under the skin, and what the skin does when fluid collects in it.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because the inflammatory picture also involves dermal lymphatics, so the two feel like one mechanism.
The orange-peel sign alone does not need the inflammatory picture. Emboli in dermal lymphatics define inflammatory cancer, and that needs the red, warm breast.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate a sign from the syndrome it sometimes belongs to.

say.text: Yes. Blocked subdermal lymphatics cause skin oedema, which pulls the skin pores down and makes the orange-peel look.
Skin involvement alone does not make inflammatory cancer. The inflammatory picture is a whole-breast syndrome.
A red, warm, swollen breast, with orange-peel skin over a third of it and no discrete lump.
What is the T category?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check the whole breast, not just the skin: how much of it is red, warm and swollen, and whether a lump is there to find.
That is not the right choice.
It is tempting because peau d'orange puts a tumour in T4b, so the skin sign feels like the whole answer.
Skin involvement is one route to T4. Here the whole breast is red, warm and swollen, so the clinical picture decides the category.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the skin sign from the clinical picture that decides the T category.

say.text: Yes. Inflammatory carcinoma is T4d: red, warm and swollen, with peau d'orange over at least a third of the breast.
Skin alone is not enough for T4d; the whole picture is.
